Read the passage and answer the question.

Yoga, which has its roots in ancient Indian philosophy, was recognised as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2014. The International Day of Yoga is observed on 21 June every year, following a resolution adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 2014 at India's initiative. Yoga combines physical postures, breathing exercises, meditation, and ethical disciplines to promote holistic well-being.

According to the passage, which body adopted the resolution declaring 21 June as International Yoga Day?

options.option_text: UNESCO, which also recognised Yoga as Intangible Heritage
The United Nations General Assembly, at India's initiative
The World Health Organisation, in collaboration with India
The UN Security Council, following an Indian government proposal

questions.explanation: B is correct. The passage explicitly states: 'following a resolution adopted by the United Nations General Assembly in 2014 at India's initiative.' Option A is the classic trap — UNESCO appears in the passage but only in connection with the Intangible Cultural Heritage recognition, not the Yoga Day resolution. Students who skim confuse the two distinct facts in the same sentence cluster. Grammar rule: In specific-detail questions, identify the precise grammatical subject of the relevant clause. Here the clause 'a resolution adopted by the UNGA' has UNGA as the agent — UNESCO is the agent of a different clause. Another example: 'The prize, funded by Sweden, was announced by the Norwegian Committee' — Sweden ≠ announcer.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Soil is often called the 'skin of the Earth,' yet it is one of the most overlooked natural resources. The top layer, known as topsoil, is the most fertile and is formed over thousands of years through the weathering of rocks and the decomposition of organic matter. Deforestation, overgrazing, and unsustainable farming practices accelerate soil erosion, stripping the land of its ability to support plant life and threatening food security worldwide.

In the passage, the word 'accelerate' most nearly means?

options.option_text: To reduce or slow down the pace of a damaging process
To speed up or intensify the rate of an ongoing process
To study and record the stages of a natural phenomenon
To reverse or undo the harmful effects of human activity

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Accelerate' derives from Latin 'accelerare' (ad + celerare — to quicken, from celer meaning swift). In context, human activities 'speed up soil erosion.' Option A (reduce/slow down) is the antonym of accelerate — students confuse 'accelerate' with 'decelerate,' a classic vocabulary trap. Substitution test — replace each option back into the sentence: 'Deforestation speeds up soil erosion' is meaningful and negative; 'Deforestation reduces soil erosion' contradicts the passage's warning tone. Grammar rule: Vocabulary-in-context questions are solved by substitution — insert each option into the original sentence and select the one that preserves both the literal meaning AND the author's tone (here: negative/threatening).

Read the passage and answer the question.

Community radio stations, unlike commercial broadcasters, are owned and operated by local communities and are mandated to serve the informational and cultural needs of a specific geographic area. In India, community radio licences are issued only to educational institutions, Krishi Vigyan Kendras, and registered civil-society organisations — not to individuals or private companies. These stations broadcast in local languages, covering agriculture, health, gender rights, and disaster alerts, acting as a last-mile communication channel.

Which inference can be logically drawn from the passage?

options.option_text: Community radio earns more advertising revenue than commercial broadcasters
A private media corporation cannot legally obtain a community radio licence in India
Community radio audiences consist exclusively of farmers and rural agricultural workers
Educational institutions pay higher licence fees compared to Krishi Vigyan Kendras

questions.explanation: B is correct. The passage states licences are issued 'only to educational institutions, Krishi Vigyan Kendras, and registered civil-society organisations — not to individuals or private companies.' The word 'only' restricts eligibility; inferring that a private corporation is excluded is a direct logical deduction. Option C is an over-generalisation — agriculture is one of several topics listed alongside health, gender rights, and disaster alerts. Options A and D introduce financial comparisons entirely absent from the passage. Grammar rule: In inference questions, the conclusion must be necessarily true (not merely possible). The presence of restricting words like 'only,' 'exclusively,' 'must,' and 'solely' in the passage are your strongest inference triggers — identify them first.

Read the passage and answer the question.

Gond art, practised by the Gond tribal community of central India — primarily in Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, and Telangana — is characterised by intricate patterns of dots and dashes used to fill images of animals, trees, and deities. Unlike Madhubani, which uses natural dyes on paper or cloth, traditional Gond art was painted on the walls and floors of homes to invite good fortune. Contemporary Gond artists such as Jangarh Singh Shyam have brought this art form to canvas and international galleries.

According to the passage, what distinguishes traditional Gond art from Madhubani in terms of medium?

options.option_text: Gond art uses natural dyes on paper, whereas Madhubani is painted on cave walls
Madhubani uses natural dyes on paper or cloth, while Gond art was traditionally on walls
Both art forms use identical materials but originate from entirely different regions
Gond art is exclusively practised on canvas today, while Madhubani uses mud walls

questions.explanation: B is correct. The passage says: 'Unlike Madhubani, which uses natural dyes on paper or cloth, traditional Gond art was painted on the walls and floors of homes.' Option A inverts the comparison — it assigns Gond's medium (paper) to Gond and Madhubani's medium (cave walls, which is not even mentioned) — a classic subject-object swap trap. Option D confuses 'contemporary' Gond art (on canvas) with traditional practice; the question asks about traditional medium. Option C is false — the two forms are explicitly distinguished by medium. Grammar rule: Comparative-contrast passages use connectives 'unlike,' 'whereas,' 'while' — always identify WHICH subject each clause belongs to. In 'Unlike A, which does X, B does Y' — A does X, B does Y, not the reverse.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Wetlands are among the most productive ecosystems on Earth, supporting a disproportionately large number of species relative to their area. They act as natural sponges, absorbing floodwaters and recharging groundwater aquifers, and their dense vegetation filters pollutants before water reaches rivers and lakes. Despite these services, wetlands continue to be drained for agriculture and urban development. The Ramsar Convention, an international treaty adopted in 1971, provides a framework for their conservation and sustainable use globally.

The author's primary purpose in writing this passage is most likely to?

options.option_text: Urge governments to immediately halt all urban development near wetland zones
Highlight wetlands' ecological value while acknowledging the threats they face
Explain step-by-step procedures for registering a site under the Ramsar Convention
Compare the productivity of wetlands with that of coral reefs and tropical rainforests

questions.explanation: B is correct. The passage describes wetland functions (flood absorption, filtration, biodiversity), notes threats (draining for agriculture/development), and mentions the Ramsar Convention — a balanced informational structure. Option A overstates: the author notes threats but does not advocate halting all development ('urge' and 'immediately halt' are too strong for the passage's neutral tone). Option C is wrong — the passage only names the Ramsar Convention; it never describes its registration procedures. Option D introduces a comparison with coral reefs and rainforests that is entirely absent. Grammar rule: 'Author's purpose' questions require distinguishing describe/inform (neutral verbs: highlight, explain, discuss) from argue/persuade (strong verbs: urge, demand, criticise). Scanning for modal intensity in the passage — does the author use 'must,' 'should,' 'ought'? — quickly reveals persuasive intent if present.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

The placebo effect is well documented: patients who receive inert treatments often experience genuine physiological improvement, driven by expectation and belief. Less studied is its mirror image — the nocebo effect — wherein negative expectations produce real adverse outcomes. A patient warned of side effects by a doctor may experience those very symptoms even from a sugar pill. This raises an ethical dilemma for informed consent: full disclosure of risks is legally mandated, yet the act of disclosure can itself generate the harm it describes. The nocebo effect thus challenges the assumption that more information is invariably beneficial to the patient.

The phrase 'invariably beneficial' in the final sentence most precisely conveys which meaning?

options.option_text: Occasionally helpful to patients who actively seek transparent medical information
Beneficial without exception in every conceivable clinical or informational context
Partially useful when disclosed only by a licensed and qualified medical practitioner
Broadly beneficial when paired with supportive counselling from a trained therapist

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Invariably' derives from Latin 'in + variabilis' — incapable of varying, hence 'without exception in every case.' The author's argument is precisely that the nocebo effect challenges the belief that information is ALWAYS (= without exception) good; Option B captures this absolute universality. Option A (occasionally) is nearly the opposite — it weakens to a low-frequency claim, destroying the author's point. Options C and D introduce conditions (licensed practitioners, counselling) that the author never qualifies the assumption with. Grammar rule: Adverbs of frequency mark degrees of universality — invariably (100%), usually (~80%), often (~60%), sometimes (~40%), occasionally (~20%). Swapping 'invariably' for 'occasionally' reverses the logical force of the sentence entirely. Similarly: 'Exercise is invariably good' ≠ 'Exercise is occasionally good.'

Read the passage and answer the question.

Microfinance institutions (MFIs) extend small loans to individuals — predominantly women in rural areas — who lack access to formal banking. While MFIs have been celebrated for promoting financial inclusion, critics argue that high interest rates, sometimes exceeding 30% per annum, trap borrowers in cycles of debt rather than liberating them. Several Indian states witnessed MFI-induced debt crises in the 2000s, prompting the Reserve Bank of India to cap interest rates and mandate a cooling-off period. The tension between financial inclusion and borrower protection remains unresolved.

Which of the following, if true, would MOST weaken the critics' argument against MFIs?

options.option_text: Several MFIs reported net losses in the fiscal year following the RBI interest-rate cap
Most MFI borrowers repay loans on time and report improved household income thereafter
The RBI cooling-off rule was introduced after lobbying by formal banking institutions
Average MFI loan sizes in rural India range between ₹10,000 and ₹50,000 per borrower

questions.explanation: B is correct. The critics' core claim is that high interest rates trap borrowers in debt cycles. To weaken this, one must show borrowers are NOT trapped — i.e., they successfully repay and their financial condition improves, which Option B directly provides as counter-evidence. Option A (MFIs posting losses after rate caps) addresses the institutions' profitability, not borrower outcomes — irrelevant to the debt-trap claim. Option C questions the RBI's motivation but provides no data on whether debt traps actually occur. Option D (average loan size) is neutral quantitative data — knowing loans are ₹10k–₹50k says nothing about whether borrowers escape or enter debt cycles. Grammar rule: 'Weaken the argument' questions follow a two-step protocol — (1) precisely identify the CONCLUSION being attacked (here: debt cycles occur due to high rates), then (2) find the option that provides evidence the conclusion is FALSE, not merely evidence that questions a supporting premise or introduces unrelated data.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Yoga, rooted in ancient Indian philosophy, has transcended cultural boundaries to become a global wellness practice. Recognised by the United Nations through the declaration of 21 June as International Yoga Day in 2015, it combines physical postures, controlled breathing, and meditation to promote holistic health. Unlike gym-based fitness routines that target only physical strength, yoga nurtures the mind-body connection, reducing stress and improving concentration. Its adaptability — from gentle restorative yoga for elderly practitioners to vigorous Ashtanga sequences for athletes — has made it universally accessible.

What is the primary purpose of this passage?

options.option_text: To compare yoga with gym-based fitness routines in terms of effectiveness
To describe the physical postures involved in Ashtanga yoga sequences only
To explain yoga's Indian origins and its worldwide appeal as a holistic practice
To argue that meditation is more effective than physical exercise for mental health

questions.explanation: C is correct. RC rule for main-idea questions: identify the controlling idea that ALL sentences in the passage collectively support, not a detail confined to a single sentence. Every sentence here — UN recognition, health benefits, and adaptability — supports yoga's global holistic appeal. Option A is tempting because the passage mentions gym routines, but that comparison is only one supporting point, not the overarching purpose. Option B is wrong because Ashtanga is cited only as one example of adaptability. Option D overstates the passage — yoga 'nurtures the mind-body connection' but the author never declares it categorically superior to physical exercise. Applying the rule to another context: if a passage covers rivers' sources, courses, and economic importance, the main idea is rivers' significance to civilisation, not merely their sources.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

The Sundarbans, shared between India and Bangladesh, is the world's largest tidal mangrove forest. Spread across approximately 10,000 square kilometres, it serves as a critical carbon sink and a natural buffer against cyclones and storm surges that frequently batter the Bay of Bengal coastline. The forest is also home to the Royal Bengal Tiger, one of the apex predators uniquely adapted to swimming between mangrove islands. However, rising sea levels caused by climate change and encroaching human settlements have significantly reduced its coverage over the past century.

According to the passage, what role do the Sundarbans play during cyclones?

options.option_text: They function as a natural shield that absorbs storm surges and cyclone impact
They redirect cyclonic winds towards the open sea away from the coastlines
They generate coastal rainfall that weakens cyclone intensity before landfall
They alert coastal communities by amplifying wave-height readings in advance

questions.explanation: A is correct. RC rule for detail questions: scan for the keyword 'cyclone' in the passage, then read the surrounding clause precisely. The passage states the Sundarbans serve as 'a natural buffer against cyclones and storm surges' — 'buffer' is a noun meaning a protective barrier that absorbs impact, making option A the correct paraphrase. Option B introduces redirecting winds, which is not stated anywhere in the passage. Option C introduces rainfall generation, equally absent. Option D fabricates a wave-height warning function. SSC and IBPS RC tests frequently reward paraphrase-matching: 'natural buffer' → 'natural shield that absorbs impact'. Applying the rule: if a passage says a dam acts as 'a regulator of water flow', the correct answer to 'What does the dam do?' is 'controls water release', not 'generates electricity', even if dams generally do that.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Urban heat islands emerge when natural land cover is replaced by dense concentrations of pavements, buildings, and other heat-absorbing surfaces. This phenomenon makes cities significantly warmer than surrounding rural areas — sometimes by as much as 5°C. The consequences are manifold: increased energy consumption for air conditioning, worsening air quality, and heightened risk of heat-related illnesses, particularly among the elderly and outdoor labourers. Mitigation strategies include planting green corridors, installing reflective rooftops, and mandating greenery quotas in new construction projects.

The word 'manifold' as used in the passage means most nearly —

options.option_text: Clearly visible and easily measurable through standard quantitative data
Severe in intensity and directly linked to health outcomes and fatalities
Unpredictable in occurrence and difficult to reverse once they emerge
Numerous and varied in their nature, affecting many different domains of life

questions.explanation: D is correct. RC vocabulary rule — context-substitution: replace 'manifold' with each option inside the original sentence 'The consequences are manifold: increased energy consumption…, worsening air quality…, and heightened risk…'. Three distinct, different-domain consequences follow the colon, matching 'numerous and varied'. Word-formation note: 'manifold' derives from Old English 'manigfeald' (manig = many + feald = fold/times), the same root that gives engineering its 'manifold' (a pipe with multiple outlets). Option A fails because the passage does not discuss measurability. Option B is tempting since health risk is mentioned, but 'manifold' modifies all three consequences collectively, not just their severity. Option C introduces unpredictability, which is never discussed. Applying the rule: 'The applications of solar energy are manifold: electricity generation, water heating, and desalination' — here too, manifold = numerous and varied across domains.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Khadi, the hand-spun and hand-woven cloth popularised by Mahatma Gandhi during the freedom struggle, was far more than a fabric. It was a political statement — a call to boycott British-manufactured textiles and to revive indigenous cottage industries that colonial policies had systematically dismantled. Gandhi believed that spinning the charkha daily was a meditative act that united diverse communities across caste and class lines. Post-independence, however, khadi struggled commercially as mill-made fabrics offered cheaper, more uniform alternatives. Recent years have seen a dramatic revival, driven partly by government promotion and partly by a global appetite for sustainable, handmade fashion.

Which of the following can be reasonably inferred from the passage?

options.option_text: Khadi's current revival is entirely due to government promotion schemes alone
Khadi's post-independence commercial decline was linked to cost and uniformity
Gandhi promoted khadi primarily to introduce meditation into daily public life
British manufacturers adopted hand-spinning techniques to undercut Indian weavers

questions.explanation: B is correct. RC inference rule: a valid inference is strongly implied by the stated facts without importing outside knowledge or overstating the passage. The passage directly states 'mill-made fabrics offered cheaper, more uniform alternatives' — thus cost and uniformity drove the decline. This follows tightly from what is written. Option A uses the absolute word 'entirely' — the passage says the revival is 'partly by government promotion and partly by global appetite', so attributing it wholly to government is an overstatement. This 'entirely/only' trap is a classic SSC CGL distractor. Option C distorts the passage — Gandhi described the charkha act as meditative, but his explicit primary purpose was economic boycott and political resistance. Meditation was a secondary characterisation, not the goal. Option D is wholly fabricated; the passage never mentions British manufacturers adopting Indian techniques. Applying the inference rule: if a passage says 'sales fell after prices doubled', the inference 'higher prices hurt demand' is valid; inferring 'the company went bankrupt' is not.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Groundwater depletion in India has reached a crisis point that policy documents acknowledge but implementation rarely addresses. Across the Indo-Gangetic plains, farmers extract water at rates far exceeding natural recharge, lured by subsidised electricity that makes pumping virtually cost-free. Drip irrigation technologies exist; crop-diversification schemes have been announced; watershed management programmes have received funding. Yet aquifer levels continue to fall year after year. One is left wondering whether the will to act matches the urgency of the data.

The author's tone in this passage is best described as —

options.option_text: Optimistic, implying that drip irrigation and funded programmes will eventually succeed
Neutral and detached, presenting factual data without any editorial perspective
Concerned and critical, questioning the gap between policy awareness and action
Alarmist, predicting an imminent irreversible collapse of India's water resources

questions.explanation: C is correct. RC tone-identification rule: locate evaluative language — word choices that signal approval, disapproval, or doubt — rather than neutral descriptors. Here, 'rarely addresses', 'Yet aquifer levels continue to fall', and the rhetorical question 'One is left wondering whether the will to act matches the urgency of the data' all signal concern and implicit criticism of inaction. Option A is wrong — solutions like drip irrigation are listed only to contrast them with continuing decline; they are not presented as hopeful outcomes. Option B is wrong because the rhetorical question at the end is unmistakably editorial, not neutral reporting — it passes judgement on the gap between knowledge and action. Option D overstates — 'alarmist' requires predictions of catastrophic, irreversible outcomes; the author criticises inertia but does not predict total collapse. The concerned/alarmist distinction is a frequent HARD-difficulty trap. Applying the rule: 'Despite policy reforms, air quality indices remain poor — one must ask if these measures are more than symbolic' = concerned/critical, not alarmist.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

The debate over classical music and cognitive development has generated contradictory findings. Early studies, enthusiastically dubbed the 'Mozart Effect', suggested that listening to Mozart temporarily enhanced spatial reasoning scores. The popular press transformed this modest laboratory finding into a sweeping claim: that exposing infants to classical music would permanently boost intelligence. Toy manufacturers rushed to market 'Baby Einstein' products. Subsequent rigorous meta-analyses, however, found that active music training — learning to play an instrument — produced modest but real gains in phonological awareness and working memory, while passive listening conferred no lasting benefit. The distinction between doing and hearing, it turns out, matters enormously.

Which of the following titles best captures the central argument of the passage?

options.option_text: 'Mozart Effect: How Classical Music Permanently Boosts Infant Intelligence'
'Active Musical Training vs. Passive Listening: What the Research Actually Shows'
'The Reckless Commercialisation of Classical Music Claims by Toy Companies'
'Meta-Analyses: The Only Reliable Method in Cognitive Development Research'

questions.explanation: B is correct. RC rule for title questions: a suitable title must capture the dominant argument — the claim the entire passage builds toward — not a sub-point or illustrative detail. The passage's logical arc is: Mozart Effect (passive listening) was overhyped → popular press amplified it → meta-analyses refuted it → active training, not passive listening, yields real cognitive benefit. Every paragraph serves the distinction between active and passive musical engagement. Option A restates the debunked popular myth — the passage argues against this position, making A a trap for careless readers who stopped at the first paragraph. Option C focuses on toy manufacturers, which is one illustrative sentence, not the central argument. Option D overclaims — the passage cites meta-analyses as more rigorous evidence but never asserts they are the 'only' reliable method. The key skill tested here is distinguishing the position the passage dismantles (A) from the conclusion it reaches (B). Applying the rule: if a passage traces how handwashing was once mocked but later proven to prevent infection, the title is 'From Ridicule to Proof: The Science of Handwashing', not 'Why Doctors Once Rejected Handwashing'.

questions.stem:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Proponents of four-day work weeks argue that reducing working hours does not reduce productivity — it may even increase it. Pilot programmes in Iceland and New Zealand reported that employees completed the same volume of work in fewer hours, with lower stress and higher job satisfaction. The reduced commute days also contributed to a measurable decline in employees' carbon footprint. Critics, however, contend that such results are difficult to replicate in manufacturing, healthcare, or retail sectors where physical presence and service continuity are non-negotiable. They also warn that a compressed schedule may simply shift overwork rather than eliminate it.

Which of the following, if true, would most effectively WEAKEN the argument made by the proponents of the four-day work week?

options.option_text: Several technology companies in the pilot programmes reported higher annual revenue
Employees in the pilot programmes showed no significant change in overall sleep quality
Commute reduction during the trials led to a measurable fall in transport emissions
A majority of pilot participants were knowledge-sector workers in office-based roles

questions.explanation: D is correct. RC critical-reasoning rule for 'weaken' questions: identify the scope of the proponents' claim (that reduced hours broadly boost productivity), then find the option that reveals the evidence base is unrepresentative of that scope. If pilot participants were overwhelmingly office-based knowledge workers, the findings cannot be generalised to manufacturing, healthcare, or retail — precisely the sectors critics flag as non-replicable. This is the classic 'biased sample' weakener. Option A actively strengthens the proponents' case by adding revenue evidence. Option B concerns sleep quality, which is irrelevant to the productivity claim — the proponents argue about work output, not personal wellness metrics. Option C also strengthens the proponents' carbon-footprint benefit claim. The sophistication of D lies in not directly asserting 'productivity fell' — instead it undermines the generalisability of the evidence itself. Rhetorical-grammar note: 'if true' signals a hypothetical critical-reasoning format common in advanced IBPS PO and CAT RCs, requiring students to evaluate logical impact rather than factual accuracy — a skill distinct from straightforward detail or inference questions.
